THE HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT

Without delay toe coronation serloce ne• gam The Archbishop in loud voice presented the King to the iissembled .people, crying, "Sirs. I here present unto you King George. the undmilded King of this Realm; where• fore all yon who are come this day to do your homage and service. are you willing to do the same!" From the Westminster scholar+ came ' the response. "God Save King George!" while trumpets blared forth an emphatio !mean. The Litany, part ilf the Communion, Seiviee and the Sermon preached, short and to the point. by the Archbishop of York, (id- , lowed, and then the King walked forward to take and sign the Oath. The hymn. "Vent, Creator Spiritu,s," preceded the first solemn net of the CorAnation, the great eccleeiastical rite of Anointing. The King, divested of his ' crimson rube attn cap, seated himself in the historic King Edward's Chair. A canopy of cloth of gold. supported by Lord Rosebery, Lord Catliman, Lord Crewe, and Lord Minto, wan heid over him, and he was anointed with oil by the Archbishop on head, handa, and breast. The aupertunica of cloth of gold an. placed upon his Majesty, his heels were touched with the golden spurs, the sword in the scabbard of purple velvet WllB girt upon him, and then offered at the altar, the Orb and the Sceptres delivered to him, and theta, clad in the pall of gold; the King seated himself in the chair for the crowning. With Moiety dignity the Archbishop placed the Crown 011 the King'a bead while ahouts of

God Save the lerng!"—ti;d this; time eon. libed to Westminster scholars echoed through the nave, and the assembled Peers placed their coronets on their heads The great set van impressively performed— dignity and reverence were in every move- ment of the King. The Archbishop knelt on the steps before the King and did homage, kissing his Majesty's left cheek. Then earns the Prince of Wales. The Duke of Con- naught andi the Peers followed, and at the end the drum. lintke (nut again, and the cry of "Long Live King George!"

The ceremony of anointing, crowning, and enthroning the Queen was then proceeded with. Her Canopy was held by four tall Duchesses (Montrose. Portland, Sutherland, and Hamilton!, and her procession to the Altar and back to the throne was a very bril- liant spectacle. The Communion Service was proceeded with, and then the choir sang the Fe Denim." while their Majesties turned into St. Edward's Chapel. The service was over—half an hour before it had been expec- ted to close—and now there remained the recession. In the same stately order that she came steal Queen Marc. tints time to the strains of the National Anthem, and genuine shouts of "God Save the Queen!" from all sides. Then after an interval King George passed slowly from the Abbey. As be passed Into sight of the nave from under the screen a great hoarse shout of welcome went up. it was the Knights of his Empire. the men of Australia and India. Canada and Ceylon, the 'errant, of Great Britain in the uttermost parts of the earth, the sailors and the soldiers making their homage and gi•ing their vow of fealty to their newly-crowned Monarch.

A 'Orion! mishap occurred during tile( ao011,;,0 festivities at Barnstaple and ihe ci•ic prod...ion came very neer to being involved is it. "f Ler accideet was tire blowing dean ore large orearnenini arch, forty lent high, and one woman way killed on the ens% .N•.mbere of oiler ritc.alcis rst,ta'nol lii Ito 1.m.3.

ing of the King. He is King by virtue of birth and becomes King from the moment of the death of his predecessor. Nor is it his public recognition. The Coronation is really the consecration of the King to the service of the State and upon this idea the service is framed.

On the morning of Coronation day the Ampulla filled with anointing oil is placed with the ancient anointing spoon upon the Abbey altar. The Archbisops and attendant Bishops wait for the King and Queen at the great west door and conduct them to chairs placed before their thrones near the altar. They walk to the strains of the anthem " I was glad when they said unto me, we will go into the house of the Lord."

that an individual was set apart to a high calling. Thus were Saul, David, Solomon and Josiah recognised as rulers. The famous vessel used in the Abbey was fashioned- 800 years ago, and is shaped like an eagle. From the eagle's mouth the oil is poured into a spoon and the sign of a cross is made upon the King's head and breast and hands. Whilst the Archbishop repeats " Be thou anointed with holy oil as kings, priests, and prophets were anointed, and as Solomon was anointed King by Zodak the priest and Nathan the prophet so be you anointed, blessed and consecrated King over this people whom the Lord your God hath given you to rule and govern. In the name of the Father, and of the son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen." The strains of the fine old hymn " Come Holy Ghost our hearth inspire" are sung and the king takes his place in the famous coronation chair made by the first Edward in the year 1300. The Anointing and the hymn indicate by symbol.the fervent hope that the Spirit of God may enrich the Spirit of the ruler and fit him for his great destiny. THE INVESTURE.

Though having less of religious association the placing of the King in his symbolical robes and the giving of the sword and orb are no less religious in their intent. First he is placed in a garment of white, soon after the Armill, a garment of clerical pattern is given,and this is surmounted by the Imperial robe. If symbol means anything the King by his priestly garments is made "God's minister." He is to be God's executioner too for as the sword is belted around him he is exhorted to" do justice, stop the growth of iniquity, protect the Holy Church of God, punish, reform what is amiss and confirm what is in good order." The Orb is next given, which is a globe surmounted by a Cross and with it comes the reminder from the Arch- bishop that" the whole world is subject to the Power and Empire of Christ our Redeemer." 01 the same nature is the ring which is placed upon the finger. The Royal Signet has a cross engraved upon it and the Primate prays that the Monarch may be "sealed with the spirit of promise." The Sceptre, the token of kingly power, and the Rod with the Dove, the symbol of mercy and equity, are held in the hands and last of all the Archbishop takes the Crown.

div.head: – – – – – – -- ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
div.p: - - - - - - -- ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.
THE RELIGIOUS SIDE OF THE CORONATION.

" Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed Solomon king." To-day we get on without Nathan the prophet, and Zadok the priest looms large upon the scene. For one or two brief hours the subject is above his sovereign and the throne is overshadowed by the Chu rch.Zadok has contrived through long ages to have it so, and until another Nathan arises as courageous as the first, he may be trusted so to keep it. No, it is not Parliament that arranges the Coronation; it is the Archbishop. A plucky Nathan he will have to be when he arises to get back the place he loot at the King's right hand.

But this is hardly the time to discuss the merits of priest and prophet. The ceremonial is over and all the traditims have been kept. We propose to till a small niche in the great fabric of journalistic Coronation effort by describing the scriptural basis of Coronation ritual. .
There is scarcely a ceremonial that is built more carefully upon scriptural precedent than that which confirms a British monarch to his throne.

It is true that surprisingly little is recorded in the Bible concerning the crowning of kings. At first it is the Prophet alone who is the king-maker. Samuel anoints Saul and gives him the kiss of benediction. Then it is young David who receives the anointing oil from the same hand. These ceremonies are entirely religious and not secular and in the same light we may regard the solemn recog- nition of Solomon. But hero the priest has claimed a place and in the course of the ages he has made his place so large that the prophet with whom the function begun has been palled from sight. It is to the Coronation of the little Prince Joash that we must turn if we would find the model upon which our fathers based the service we use to-day. Brought from con- cealment by his good nurse and saved by her from the fury of Athaliah he was the subject of a series of interesting ceremonies. The six-year-old boy was lifted before the people and a covenant recorded. Then he was crowned and anointed and into his hands was placed the "Testimony.' a portion of the Old Testament writings. And, whilst the musicians did their best, the people cried "God save the King." Let us see how faithfully these doings have been reproduced to-day. THE RECEPTION. . .
The Coronation, of course, ie not the tnak

div.head: RECOGNITION.
div.p: THE RECOGNITION.

The King and Queen stand upon a platform called the theatre (a term quite appropriate for the Greek word theatre means simply a spectacle) and the Archbishop goes through a formal though significant performance. Walking slowly to the four sides of the platform, north, south, east and west, he repeats the words " I plesent unto you, , King George, the undoubted King of this realm."

Then addressing the assembly he asks for their allegiance, asking the Peers whether they will submit to the Sovereign and serve him. This follows quite strikingly the Scripture precedent and the answer is given in Biblical form" God save King George." The crowd that shouted for little Joash little thought they were setting a fashion that woull linger so long. This week,though on a grander scale, the old scene has been repeated. The trumpets blare out and the crowd without take up the cry. ' Then following an ancient custom the King makes oblation or offering to God in the form of a wedge of gold and an altar cloth.

div.head: LITANY,
div.p: THE LITANY,

lithe shout flavours of what is secular the impression is at once corrected, and the assembly is led by a rapid transition to a humble repetition of the words of the Litany. The whole assembly chants the pathetic words that ask for protection and deliveriance from evil, an this leads to the obserliance of the service of Holy Communion. The brief sermon follows and the monarch is now asked to take the volemn oath.

div.head: OATH
div.p: THE OATH

Kneeling on the steps of the altar and with a volume before him containing the Gospels, the King places his hand on the open page and takes a pledge of fidelity to the nation, the Empire and the Constitution, the oath including a vow of allegiance to the Protes- tant faith. With the words "The things which I have here before promised, I will perform and keep, So help me God" he kisses the Bible and signs the oath. THE ANOINTING.
To us a smearing of oil would convey no religious suggestion, but it was anciently the symbol of consecration and the outward sign

div.head: CORONATION.
div.p: THE CORONATION.

The Crown rests upon Ai altar and the Primate' lifts it to place upon the King's head. But he immediately lay it in its place again, in token that it belongs to God, that only by Him kings are allowed to rule and that to God it will be returned in His own time. Lifting it a second time it is placed upon the King's head and again the Abbey echoes to the cry "God Save the King.

div.head: BIBLE.
div.p: THE BIBLE.
The Bible is next taken from the altar and given to His Majesty with words of admonition that it be his guide and heavenly dictator.
The Bendiction closes this series of symbolical acts, but another feature remains to give climax to the whole.

div.head: ENTHRONEMENT
div.p: THE ENTHRONEMENT
When Joash as a six-year boy stood before the throne it was from convenience, perhaps from necessity, that they" lifted "him upon
t. Very strangely they would have been mpressed could they have known that in onsequence full grown monarchs would be _ . .

lifted tong ages 'lifter to their royal seats. It is here perhaps more than in any other detail that we see how entirely the Church has followed scriptural precedent. The King is "lifted" to his throne by the bishops and archbishops who afterwards do homage kissing his cheek as Samuel kissed the cheek of Saul on the Palestinal hillside long ago. We have only set ourselves to point to the religious side of the Coronation and can omit mention of the nuniberless details that distract attention from its outstanding features and dim its true meaning. The Coronation service attests in the language of symbol, ritual and prayer the truth " By Me Kings rule and princes decree justice," and its high nieanin4is voiced in the prayer that accompanies the crown "As Thou dost this day set .11 crown of pure gold upon his head, so enrich his Royal heart with Thine abundant grace, and crown him with all princely virtues through the King Eternal.

div.head: CORONATION.
div.p: THE CORONATION.

How shall we crown the King? With a great diadem of gents sod gold, Reit rubies, sapphire. bluer than the sky, Rice emerald., and dimly. ode manifold, Pearls, milky opals, lapis lazuli? They might be proud to cling About the brows of Alfred's laid... heir, The royal offspring of • thiusend years, Greet Edward's denoting sceptre born to bear, Whose shining memory all the world reveres. div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING. By Redcap.) THE SWAN.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING. By Redcap.) THE SWAN.

This is coronation week, and a ' few lines about the 'Royal Water-foal" may not be out of place. It hardly tomes within the realms of practical pml,ry farming. Nevertheless. you will donbtlees pardon me for giving my weekly co,uron a royal touch at this festive season. With the permission of the edi,or and the kind tolerance of my many readers, I shall ask them to accept the follow- ing few rotes from the pen of that great lover of poultry ,airl a great artist), the late Mr. Ilsrrison Weir. In his Our Poultry," he writes as follow. on the royal swan : —The swan, both for its elegance, its usefulnerta, and as a standard dish at royal and civic banquet., has, front an early period been held in the highest esteem. It is at once an ornament to our lake and rivets, and the admira- tion of young and old ; while also that which is delicate to the touch is revealed by the analogy that it is" an soft as swans' down," and our best beloved poet and tuaster-mind was not inaptly called " the sweet swan of Avon," and himself, too, noted —who noted all things well—" the swans' down feather " t" Anthony and Cleopatra," Act 11. sc. ii ; arid again, of the love of the mother swan be says, " So doth the ewan her downy cygnets save . . . . ." Often he tells of its nature, its habits, in trutlifnl word* in many ways, even to its haunts and homes, when in ",Cymbeline " (Act 111. Sc. .1) he pictmes "in a great poo! a swans' nest." Other poet, have loved the swan, but none knew it like Shakespeare. And then Mr. Weir g,es on ta say that "the swan was ever a Royal bird, and in the twenty- second year of Edward IV. (or it enacted that "no person anho did not p Axles a free- hold of a clear yearly rental of live marks," was permitted to keep any." So much then about the Royal swan. It is only right that of all the feathered tribe, the swan should be so specially selected as the Royal bird. It is beautiful ! Its majestic forni,— when softly gliding over the lake—almost suggests "Regentship " of the water.
rift I ri Nl.Olll/11.

Queen Alexander was a great lover of poultry at one time, especially so with regard to exhibition birds Her aside often figured in the prize lists of some of the best shoss in the kingdom. So you see that we can boast of Rosal patronage in our poultry pursuits. I have thought, therefore, that whi!e nearly every column will be tinged with royalty, why not our poultry column ? There is not the least doubt —but that we shall still be so honoured with Royal patronage in the future reign as we have Ivan in the past. Ileauwhile we can say, "God save the King .and Queen."
Tim BREEDING. REASON.

The breeding season is just drawing O a close. Except for the resrinc of table poultry, it is not wise to set any eggs after June. because if you do, it means that you oil have difficulty in getting the young stock sufficiently well-grown (to be profitable) ere the bad weather seta in. Then again it is unwise to rear pullets late on in the season for next season's breeding pens. So I should reconunend you now to concentrate all your efforts on the young stock now existing.

01TINO rim 0E 00. It is very iniprtant thdt this should be done as early as they are diecernable. As a result they grow and come on in every respect much more quickly than if left al mined together. By now you should be able to sort out the best of the early batched .•orkerels. Tho..e which do not come up to the standard in all-round quality should liedicardet, tel up, arid killed off. Do not era.te your span and time by keeping inferior stock. Besides you will 511,3 a great deal in the corn bill by so doing.
tIII: lowNo -111 1

Great rare 'Mould be taken of the early pullets. Ito not overfeed dr. m or they nil come on to lay at too early an age. Vim shou'l never induce pullets to lay until you one satisfied that they are fully matured. Feed them sparingly on a pond sample of wheat with an occasional soft feed of biscuit meal and thirds. II they are kept in confine- merit see that you give them an ample supply of green food. Of course these directions must apply only to those fairly well matured. The younger ones von must keep on the mme. Feed them , regilarly on nutritious food-stuffs, not forgetting tho value of meat in some fmin. To those who cannot afford a green bone mini, then an occaaioual feed on boiled bullock's liver (chopped fine) will act nearly as 'well. Keep the drinaing water well supplied —this is Cu irnrortant—on very hit days it soon becomes : tainted and there is nothing much worse for them than foul water.
IMEN•.

If you have selected a few of the best (with the intention of exhibiting them) these should have special attention. You must not hope for success in the ,how pen if you allow show specimens to run haphazard with the rest of the flock. What you want is • few cockerel pens dotted ale ut the farm ; and let them occupy these so that they are protected from weather condi- tions and also from fighting with the rest of the stock (especially young tockerelad These latter are like ' young onea 'in anything else. They all think they are masters until they liar." tried their luck." linfortundtely this system often spoils them in some way from growing into decent show bird.. l'se the d:ckerel pens arid move them about each day on to freah ground. In the case of pullets you may run two or even three togrther. But never more than one cockerel in each pen. I write in this manner so as to help the amateur. The old hands need no warning from n.e. They know all the arts of the fancy and this is one It is not often that you cm get a predominance of show birds in one breeding season, so do not think that you will want a great deal of accommodation for these. If you think that during the sea-on you have bred a few good birds, get au expert to look over your stock and select them for you. If you are at a loss to know who, well, lam okayu at your service and would be only too pleased to do it or you. Almoit every village flower chow caters now for poultry classes. ; therefore Iliac. thought that if I can help you to win a few prizes by adopting some of these methods -you are indeed welcome.

It is always more or lees painful to roe when the time corn, round each reason to say goodbye. How- ever it is no again, and next week I shall write the last article for the present season. I have been requested to do so in calor,. lar form for the remaining months of the year. This is a good idea because it forms a handy guide for the real of the season. Next Ai eek I shall have completed 78 columns on poultry farming, and I have to thank all those who have helped my to make the subject interesting to all.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME

The programme submitted to the patrons of the Palace and Hippodrome tics week has the commend- able gift if " infinite variety," for every class of item Bruns tO lit contained in it. Cettaby no difficulty ariTes as to our choicn of the premier 'turn, but thew, iter confesses that he is in a quandary as to which he should designate as the mo-t popular turn. However, it may frilly be urged t tint'• The Sleepwalker ' presented in characteristic fashion by Walter Ellis and Co,, finds favour with all sec,ot,u cf the lionse. The sketch which involve, three actors— two lathe.: and one gentleman—is subtly comvived, cne in which the ronwarbulistic ramblings of the governess throve the gentleman into • state of utter misery, enhanced by the crude temper of his wife. The Five driver., who give an exhibition of gymnastics and acrobatics, ' are a niarvellous mintett. Performing strange feats in the air only infuses them t,t do snore daring deed. on the tars. the Englishmen's inherited love cf excite- ment being completely satiated. Alice Craven, a comedir rise Ira' 1 ancashire, gets herself into the goodwill of the audience not only by the native render- ing of her bongs, but by her apparent spontaneous humour. As a novelty emilibrist Martell is superb, balancing himself on one finger and dancing on the tips of bin fingers having no terrors for Lim. I.ucy Gillett is one of the few acrobati, lady jugglers who are really clever. Her turn has also the merit of being decidedly original. I,,,Luis J. Seymour (light comedian) contributes some commendable songs, in the choruses of which the audiences enthusiastically joined. As tt,al the pictures are full of entertaining episode., and the manic supplied by the orchestra under the leadership of Mr. E. A. Widdop, is rbasir g to listen to.

div.head: BLUE COAT SCHOOL REUNION.
div.p: BLUE COAT SCHOOL REUNION.

" Old Bitten" assembled in largo numbers at this school on Sunday eveniog when the •nnual re-union ser•ice was held. They were heartily welcomed by Mr and Mrs Rom, and then spent the time before the com- mencement of the service in inspecting the buildings and the grounds, which on there occasions are ninny. thrown ripen to them. At 130 the service in the chapel commenced, the Old Blues occupying the front seats as usual. the children took their places on the gallery in the chapel, singing as a precessional, the egad. Psilm commencing" I was glad when they said into me we will go into the boiler, of the Lord." Then followed the hymns " Lift uo your heads ye lofty wites"—tte mule hymn which one sung by the Bl.i• Coat children at the old church at the opening of the present Khoo!, January 112. After the reading of the opening prayers by ooe of the pupil., 0. Appleton, a portion of Scripture front the Book of Justus wes recited from memory by C Lloyd, and then the Gospel for the dim by one of the girls, 11. L m owe. The catechism was upon '• The Three Baptismal Duties," and was followed by the anthem "0 Lord God of Hosts," by fl. E. Lyle, which col well rendered by the children, the soloist being F. J. Jones. The remaining prayers were reed by Roughley, after which a setting of the Nuno Dimittis by %Vegetal! wee sung, end the service concluded by the singing of the hymn" Lord dismisn us with Thy hlessing." Eighty Old Blues were present at the Reunion, and amongst thews were Aldermen Font's's (president of the Blue Coat Brotherly Society), Mr F Short (secretary l, Mr W Rutter (treasurer, Mm Forshaw, Mrs Short, Messrs T Armstrong bandroseter), J Armstrong, W Rowe, .1 Tilley, R C Essenbirth, T Pilling, and I W Kettle llnocoin),blri L NI illett cfliziatel as organist during he service.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SAMRDAY. JUNE 14 1911.
It must be a source of THE great satisfaction to CORONATION, the whole of the English

speaking peoples that the Coronation of KING GEORGE V. and QUEEN MARY has been consummated with so much eclat, and with an entire freedom from any incident of an untoward nature. Pessimists always indulge in gloomy fore- bodings on such occasions, but the fates were in their kindest mood on Thursday, and after the completion of the solemn ceremonials, the nation was free to rejoice in the good omens which such a day inspires—omens of Peace on earth and goodwill to men." The rejoicings have everywhere been carried out with a heartiness and abandon which almost, if not entirely, contradict the largely true statement that Englishmen take their pleasures sadly. We were reminded of this 'critical summing up of a national character- istic when we witnessed the town's and friendly societies' procession in Warrington, for imposing in some aspects as the function was, it did not convey either to the eye or the mind that the hundreds of people partici- pating were rejoiced either by the day or the 'occasion. Perhaps this is an inherent fault of processions on "feast days" of this kind. Why we should "process" at all when we wish to be merry and bright is a question which might reasonably be considered with seriousness. There are many other ways of celebrating a glad time, but they do not seem to appeal to the national temperament sufficiently to relegate processions to occasions when the aspect of things is more funereal and there is a definite goal in view. But having "processed," the people of Warrington and the country generally have betaken themselves to rejoicings with zest. Within the borough there has not been much scope for real jollification, and it may be said with truth that thP old folks have had a much better time than the young folks. Beyond our borders, however, the very best was made of the day. Each village vied with the next in :the variety and number of its sources of entertainment for young and old, and the elaborate programmes which were carried out so heartily and completely serve as a reminder of what Warrington might have

done, but did not! We have, in a previous issue, an imadverted on the paucity of Warrington's contribution to the general ebullition of gratification and joy, and we have no wish to enlarge upon a topic which is not attractive. Rather would we pay a warm tribute to the individual enthusiasm and self-sacrifice of His Worship the Mayor. Councillor Dr. Joseph has not spared his time, trouble or purse to make memorable those features of the day's doings with which he was !personally associated, and for so much at least, he deserves the warm thanks of the community. Finally, we would direct our readers' attention to the salient fact—perhaps some- what obscured to-day—that Kingship, even in this democratic Empire, remains in a great and unique position. The kingly functions have changed; old ones have become atro- phied, others have developed. But never in its whole history has the English Monarchy had greater potentialities of good than now. Leave the immense scope at home out of the question; think, of what an English Sovereign to-day may do, by the force of his personality and the attractiveness of his sentiments, for the cause of world-peace and Imperial unity. EDWARD VII. left more real mark on the world, had more real permanent influence on affairs, than many A 'so-called absolute despot who has had the lives of his subjects in the hollow of his hand. GEORGE V. already promises to be a tremendously effective binding force between the various parts of the Empire. He knows the Dominions beyond the seas personally; their peoples know him. He is a man of unflagging energy, of lofty serious- ness, of thorough conscientiousness. We feel sure that the affectionate and heartening shouts of welcome from scores of millions of his people all over the world, cannot fail to strengthen and confirm him in his resolution to face his life-work like his own courageous self, and like the ,son of his beloved father.
Mr. A. H. Croefield MR. CROSFIEU). received the hearty . .

congratulations of the Liberals of Golborne on the speech which he delivered at the opening of their new club on Saturday. It was undoubtedly a most interesting and powerful exposition of Liberal policy and touched upon the many far- reaching measures of social amelioration and reform for which the present Government has been responsible. Mr. Crosfield rightly laid great emphasis on the enormous advance of the peace movement and his whole-hearted support of the policy of amity between nations awoke a sympathetic echo in the minds of , his hearers. In the evening Mr. Crosfield I ow, again demonstrated his keen interest in I labour questions by attending a large and representative conference of trade unionists, , called to consider the proposal—which he is doing his utmost to bring within the region of practicability—for a universal eight hours day in continuous processes. On Coronation Day Mr. Crosfield took a prominent part in the local Coronation festivities and had a a very cordial greeting from the large crowd which lined the route of the town's procession. At the Town Hall his health was very heartily honoured and Mr.Crosfield, who was obviously deeply touched by the sincerity and warmth of his reception, replied in a neat speech, referring not only to his own close associations with the town but to the long and illustrious past of our loyal borough.

The Coronation List of CORONATION Honours is in itself a HONOURS. sufficient proof that the Tories never believed half they said, when they denounced a measure of reconstruction which is really rather conservative in its proposals, since it only translates constitutional custom into statute—or, in mathematical phrase, postulates into axioms—as a terrible revolution. The Tory Chief Whip goes to a Second Chamber which, if the Tory legend of even a month ago be true, will cease to exist as soon as the Parliament Bill becomes law. To pass from a point which requires no elaboration, Lord Crewe has received a marquisate as a mark of recognition for the arduous and thankless task which, as Leader of the Ministeralist ?arty in a House where the Leader of the Opposition is really the Leader of the House, he has discharged with so much tact, firmness, and skill. This is the second transformation that has taken place in the title that Lord Crewe inherited from the brilliant politician, poet, and social leader Whom mortals call Lord Houghton, but The gods call Dickey kidney," to quote from another Liberal who has combined eminence in letters—Sir G. 0. Trevelyan, one of the recipients in the Coronation List of the Order of Merit.
In a statement in the A CALUMNY House of Commons on _

' EXPLODED. Thursday, June 15th, Mr. Lloyd George effectively and finally disposed of the silly and spiteful story that the collapse of the Birkbeck Bank was due to Liber ii finance, and in particular to the Budget of 1909-10. He quoted from a statement signed by the Chief , Accountant of the Birkbeck Bank, in which the greater part of the depreciation of its securities was put down to two factors—the Boer War and the Tory legislation in 1900, which made Colonial securities trustee investments. Mr. Lloyd George took a , number of representative securities and I showed that in each the depreciation was very much heavier in the lifetime of the Tory Government.

It was in 1903 that Sir THE STEEL TRADE Joseph Brailsford told "013180." Mr,Joseph Chamberlain that it was '' erly a matter of a few months" before English steel- makers would be"crushed out of existence"by a competition which had already existed for "over three years." Less than six months before (says the "Morning Leader ") he has told his shareholders that" as a matter of fact, the five per cent dividend proposed to- day meant fifteen per cent the great majority of the shareholders, and to some of them it meant a great deal more." On the j3th. of June this year Mr. Brailsfurd admitted that every department of his works showed an increased output, that the working cost had been a good one, that a dividend of 4¢ per cent on the year had been earned (precisely the same as in 1894, and 2 per cent more than in 1895 and 1896, before "dumping" began) and that 60,000 five per cent debentures at 101 per cent had been at once subscribed by the Company's share- holders. The answer to Mr. Brailsford's complaints about the dumping of semifinished German steel is provided in a pregnant saying of Mr. Thomas Powell at the meeting of the men which met to consider the situation a week ago. "Did they expect any Govern- ment" he said " to protect 6,000 steel workers at the cost of 16,000 tinplate workers. ? " It is not rendered more probable, remarks the "Leader" by Mr. Brailsford's final admission that the company are engaged now in. negotations for a cheaper and more regular supply of ore, which, if successful," would very largely tend to the solution of the whole situation."

Only tl.ree of King George's thirty-six regal predecessors since the Conquest were crowned in the month of June—namely, I Edward IV., Henry VIII, and Victoria. But nearly all were crowned at Westminster. Henry 111. was crowned twice over, the first time at Gloucester, while Henry VI. was crowned King of France at Notre Dame: but Edward V. was never crowned at all.

Though ancient custom counts for much, there were several interesting innovations in connection with the Coronation ceremony. It is the first time that the Dominions have had their standards carried at a Coronation., Mr. Asquith was the first Prime Minister who has taken part in a Coronation procession; for till six years ago the Prime, Minister's office was "unknown to the law," and unrecognised by officiAl..ctiquette. . . e. • .; ,

That section of ihe American Press (says the" Westminster Gazette") which demands the revision of the Aldrich Tariff does not regard the decisions of the Supreme Court in the case of the Standard Oil and other trusts as the last word in the campaign against monopolies. So long as high tariffs prevent competition, the trusts, it is argued, will still be able to fleece the consumer in spite of all the decisions of the Supreme Court.

"But let the Tariff props be removed," writes the "Philadelphia Record," "and there will be an end of most of the extortions of Trust monopolies. It is now repeated, however, that like combinations exist in Free Trade England. The falsity of this assertion has been demonstrated over and over again. Such combinations cannot exist where trade is free to combat them. An effort was made in England a few years ago to form a Soap Trust, and it soon came to , grief. Its products were boycotted by British I consumers, and foreign supplies poured into I the free ports to meet the demand. The only condition on which manufacturing com- binations can succeed where trade is free is in the superior quality and cheapness of their products." • •

Why is it, asks the Christian World, that the Adult School movement does not grow more rapidly in London? The average weekly attendance of men in March was 1,800 and of women 1,558; these represent a slight decrease upon the corresponding totals of March 1910. The movement is essentially one of intensive culture, our contemporary points out, but in the Midlands it shows a greater power of growth than in London, without sacrificing in any way its personal work. There is room for a wide divergence of opinion upon the causes of this comparative slowness in London. One thing is clear, it is added: for the most part the London work- man has to be won one by one; he does not move in gangs. In Lancashire and in the Midlands there are men who will come into the Brotherhood or the Adult School in groups. There are few such groups to be won in London. . * .

A Bill to prohibit plural voting will probably be introduced, the Press Associa- tion says, after the short Parliamentary interval necessitated by the Coronation. At present, however, the matter cannot be regarded as definitely settled. It was under- stood at the beginning of the session that the Plural Voting Bill was among the "bills dealing with other . measures of importance" which were mentioned in the King's Speech as to be "introduced and pro- ceeded with as time and opportunity allow." Leading Ministers nave from time to time reiterated the strong desire of the Govern-

The Bill will, it is understood, be a short and comparatively simple one, dealing only with iplural voting at general elections. In Iprinciple it will be similar to the provision in the Local Government Act of 1888 against voting at a London County Council election in more than one of the divisions into which the county of London is divided. The larger question of preventing the effective registra- tion of voters for more than one division, as provided in Mr. Harcourt's Bill of 1906, will probably be left over.

No day in the calendar gives more genuine pleasure to the little folk and in their whole-hearted enjoyment the seniors find a world of satisfaction. But apart from i a mere sentimental aide, the festival has attractiveness which no other , local event can rival. In these aternly practicsl days, it is a relief to see something if the pictureaque occasionally, and the children's procession undoubtedly provides a pretty spectacle which even a stranger would view with in'erest and admirati a. div.p: iCHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB •..--"\e-A.1w..--‘,.."...,,,--\..,,--‘„,
THE FAMOUS DIAMOND IN THE KING'S SCEPTRE.

For the first time at a Coronation the greatest diamond in the world has flashed its beauty under the eyes of a king. In the king's sceptre has now been placed the famous Cullinen diamond and in all the regalia there is nothing more splendid. This great diamond was picked up one evening by a foreman in the Premier mine in the Transvaal. He thought he saw some- thing bright in the blue clay and cut it out with his pen-knife. It proved to he a diamond that weighed 11-3 pounds, and was of course of inestimable value. In 1907 the Transvaal Government decided that they would like to present the stone to King Edward, and upon their doing so be promised that it should he kept and preserved among the historic jewels that form the heirlooms of the Crown.

It was cut in Amsterdam with great skill and two fine stones were made from it. The one was made for the head of the sceptre and was 2 1-3 inches long and inches wide and the other was to be put in the crown. Possibly you may go to the Tower of London some day and if so you will see the fine diamonds.

It is interesting to know that when they wanted to send the huge stone to England they discussed the best methods of doing so and it was considered that the safest way would be to send it by ordinary registered post. So it was put in a box and sent off,and was delivered in the ordinary way by the , postman at one of the London Banks. THE BOY WHO RENOUNCED A CROWN.

I told you last week how in Rome they used to give crowns for all sorts of achieve- ments. This week I propose to tell you of a tine boy who won one. His name was Locus Valerius. lie lived many many years ago when Rome was mistress of the world and the Romans were braver and stronger than anyone else. He was a mere boy at the time, but he was fond of his lessons, and most of all did he love poetry. So although he was only 15 years old he made up his mind that lie would try to win the gold medal and ivory lyre which were given every five years to the boy who could write the best poem. Lucius not only tried but succeeded, and one day, before all the school and a number of visitors, the prizes were presented to him. Now, beside the medal and lyre, which everyone who gained them valued very much, there was one thing else which they thought was grander. A statue of the prize-winner was placed in the school, and crowned with laurel. You may imagine how the boy's heart beat with joy as he saw the judge step forward to crown the statue, but just at that moment Lucius caught sight of a young man who had also tried for the prize, and who looked most downcast and miserable. Lucius sprang forward, seized the laurel crown, and putting it on the head of the poor fellow who had been unsuccessful, said, " You are more deserving of it than I am. I obtained it more on account of my youth than my merit, and rather as an encouragement than a reward." Then the people set up a great shout of joy, for they knew that a noble heart was worth more than all the poems in the world, and they gave a new name to Lucius Valerium in memory of that day. Afterwards hi. was always called "Pudeus," which means modest, and you may be sure that he valued his new title as much as he deserved it, for as Lord Tennyson says: '• Kind hearts are more than coronets." CROWNING A KING.

Out on the lawn one niidaummer day Three little children grew tired of ploy; When tired of hoop, of bell, and of swing One cried," Let's play at crowning a King.' All liked the plan but could not agree. For each one wished to he king, you see, "I will IA king!" No, let me !" they cried ; At lag they asked mamma to decide. "My .•bildren, first you most understand That king should be good as well as grand; Ore to he king over all the rest Must surely be the one who is heat. "John, the client, I'll put to the vote. All hands are up but Bobbie's, I note." Then Htbie was shyly heard to nay. "John robbed a bird of her nest one day." Bobbie is • dunce, he never tie., At home or at school to gain a prize." Cried Harry, " So there is only me. Hurrah for now the king I shall be." 'Nay, not von," said John, "for I will tell That you threw little pout into the well." Each hung hi. head 'twa, a serious thing Not .e of the three wan fit tube King. •' We'll fetch baby Frank —he is only three— But is good end kind and King he shall be." on with robe and sceptre, crown, and ring They made their darling brother King ; Then they laughed and cheered, right glad to We What a gay ruler their pet could be. They merrily sang " • jolly thing This grad new game of crowning a King."

Though there was nothing elaborate about the Town's and Friendly Societies' procession, which formed the chief public event of C ironation Day, the parade was impressive by reason of the large numbers participating and its very representative character. The various civic authorities, our "citisen soldiers," those increasingly popular organizations the B Scouts and the Church Lads' lirigade —which are doing BO mach to instil discipline and a sense of responsibility into the rising generation—and the great friendly societies all had their nhare in a display which was imposing though not very beautiful. Before ten o'clock the processionists were massing on the epacious lawn in front of the Town Hall and the assembly was watched from the balcony of the civic headquarters by a large gathering of well-known Wier. and gentlemen. From all quarters came bands discoursing music, lively and serious, but chiefly of a : martial character, and the bright uniforms of the Territorials, the banners of the friendly societies and : the elaborate regalia of the officials added welcome splashes of colour to the scene. Each society had its, own appointrd marshals, but the bulk of the responsibility for seeing that all the arrangements worked smoothly rested, of course, upon the police who, under the direction of the ('hief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) liii their work perfectly. At half past ten every section if the proceseion had taken up its allotted position and the lawn was quite covered. Standing on the Town Hall balcony, the Bev E. C. E. Carleton (Mayor'e chaplain) then offered several of the epecial prayers for the King and Queen, from the commemoration service antholized by the ' Archbishops. This short religious ceremony con- cluded, the Map,ress waved a Cnion Jack and the whole of the prcceesionists, who were facing the Town }fall, sang a verse of the National Anthem, the Territorial Band giving a good lead. CANADIAN CENSUS AND REDISTRIIWTION.

One of the interesting consequences of Canada's new comma will he a re-adjustment of the member- ship of the House of Commons at Ottawa. The unit of representation is determined by the di•inion of the population of Quebec by 65, the fixed number of members guaranteed to that province under the British North America Act, and will be probably 35,01*. Thin in an increase of 8,000 over the unit on which their present Parliament was elected. On this basin it in certain that Ontario and the maritime provinces will lose some of their present represents- ' non, as the increase of population, owing to the drain of the West, has been relatively email in those provinces. On the other hand, the Western province', with n total population oil practically 2,1511,f55i, will gain an extra IS to 20 nuunbers under the new dintribut ion.

div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE PROCESSION.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE PROCESSION.
Seven Mlles of Suffragi3ts

The Voiaieair Suffrage procession in London last Saturday was a huge -times.. The lines extended, it is said, for 7 miles, and the march was never actually finished, owing to the lateness anal darkness of the hour. The Anti-Suffragists, with delicious but uncon. i scions irony, sent forth sandwichmen carrying placards with the words : "Women do not want the vote." These notices came in for the sneers and jeers of the crowd, although the sandwichmen, with sorue method in their madness, sometimes wore the placards upside down. One is grateful to Anti- Suffragists for bringing in that necessary comic . element. . . .

mvtoent. The crowd, that came to watch the procession were enormous, every available ledge iti Trafalgar Square seemed to be occupied, and there had been a run on the Coronation stands. The crowd gathered at about 3 ; the procession was only due to start at 5, and went on till after 9, so it required some patience to tsaf it to the finish. The worat of being in a Pro,ssion is that one seen so little of it. We know that it began with pageantry, impersonations of Joan of Arc, famous queens, famous women and no on, and that there was an Empire car representing the United kingdom and her colonies, bends of prisoners who amazed the London crowd, which uttered such exclamations as '"On would 'aye thought it," in shocked surprise, bands of nurses, University women in cap and gown and many coloured hoods, women doctors in scarlet and yellow and other brilliant hues, gardeners, entreats:a, artiste, writers, among them moot dis- tinguished women—but of all this we saw little.

One pretty incident on the way occurred when Mrs. Elmy, a beautiful old ladr, the aged fighter of by-gone day., who will always he remembered in connection with the Married Women's Property Act, was spied in • flower-decorated balcony to the left. Banners dipped and hands saluted, and Mn. Elmy, the fighter of a good fight, bowed her head, feeling perhaps that it wes good to have lived tone. this day, when women •re entering the prondeed land of which the old pioneers had vision.. The Warrington banner fell into line with other. of the Went Lancashire, West Cheeltire and North Wales Federation of the National Union. It was painted by Mrs. Pidduck, and was one of the prettiest in the Federation. It represents a woman in flame coloured garment, blindfolded and with scales in her hand. Behind, the grey chimney tops of Warrington show against the freahness of dawn. The row, of Lancashire stands in the two bottom corners, and a shield hears the words : " Nor attempt the future'. portal

_ With the pant'. blood-rseted key." Warrington ladies present were Miss Trude Cro. field, Miss Lucy Broadbent, Mrs. Itansome, Mrs. Simpson, Miss Hublisch and myself. The only part of the procession, of which we saw much, was that which stretched immediately in front and behind as. Among those behind were 54; women of Clither., who had given up a day's work and incurred a 3s. fine to come. One feels proud of them. Nothing was more astonishing about the procession than its representative character. It represented both sesea, all dames, from Lady Irani:es Balfour to the women of Clitharoe, all professions, and all parts of the globe. Among the colonial contingent were some I most distinguished women, wise, of men who hays come to represent their colonies at the coronation. L F. W.

div.head: CHILDREN'S SOUVENIRS.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S SOUVENIRS.
MAYOR AND MAYORESS VISIT ALL THE SCHOOLS
Picturesque Scenes---A Living Union Jack.

The day school children of Warrington played their small part in the Coronation celebrations on Wednee. day when they were re-assembled at their respective schools to receive the souvenira presented by the Corporation. The Mayor and Mayoress ((ouncillor Dr. Jr seph and Miss Joseph) made the round of the schools in • motor car and everywhere they were greeted with the utmost enthusiasm. They were accompanied by the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) and the Direct r of Education (Mr. J. Moore Murray), and a busy but most interesting day was experienced in working to the time table, which allowed only a brief stay at each school. The souvenirs take the form of a mug toils box of chocolates for each child —the total number of each class of memento being 14,000. The mug in embellished with portraits of the King and Queen and • coloured reproduction of the Borough Arms, and the chocolate box is also artistically designed and ornamented in similar style. To distribute all the gifts wax no light tank, but it was cheerfully undertaken by members of this ; The best boy and girl of each sch ol (chosen by the votes of their fellowe(holars) had the honour of receiving their souvenirs at the hands of the Mayor and Mayoress, who kindly supplemented the official Emma with .i.penee for each scholar selected for the above distinction.

At every ischool there wan a pleatting little eerernony. The Mayor, who was luntily cheered by the winder., delivered an whiyes. on leettonn of the Coronation, and the children joined in patriotic wogs.
BRILLIANT DISPLAY AT 13EA'MoNT SCHOOL.

The most elaborate spectacle of the day was teen at Bement Conned school. On entering the school yard, the visitor was impressed with a study in red, white and blue on • large scale, for all the scholarn who had mnstered in take part in the display, wore paper caps and rapes of the national colours. A brisk wind swept the ground, and now and then one of the caps would be whirled off the head of its wearer and swept high into the air. Meet of the rhildrenbow- .ever, were able to retain possession of the unaccustomed adornment, by holding them on with both hands. Near the O'Leary-street gates a guard of honour of scholarcincluding •gronp of boy scouts, was drawn up, and preparations were in progress for

I lilt he would supplement the official gift to the children not only with the usual Walking Day treat but with • pelmet to each child who attended school next Monday with a bag of sweet. and an orange. At Oor Lady's School the Mayors., received • bouquet at the hands of klias Agatha Appleton, the baby of the school. At St. James' School a special feature was the excellent singing of loyal songs, sod at the Parochial schools one of tho twat items was the Walsh song "Lend of our Fathers." Al Wycliffe and Arpley-street Schools a Coronation hymn written by Mr. A. Corney and compooed by Mr. W. fl. Payton, Mos. Bac. was sting.

div.head: Spiritualism and a Neglected Scriptural Truth
div.p: Spiritualism and a Neglected Scriptural Truth
LI 111 E 'ENV. MIkIL

Sir,—llowe refreshing it is to be able to cease from wrong ing (generally males.) and to have the pleasure of expressing a word of thanks. And this pleasure is mMe. It is no seldom that one sees M our newspapers complimentary references to the work of Spiritushat Societies that I wax inure than gratified to see in your hut week's issue that " Oltl Journalist "promo. us for having done " good eervice by insisting upon and emphasising an important scriptural truth which hu been strangely neglected by orthodok churches," There is no doubt from the Bible itself, that the early church believed in the exercise of spiritual gifts. Paul, the great apostle, in I Corinthians an, I to 11, indicates them and points out that they are all the work of the self-same Spirit. These gifts were recognized slso in the (Roman) Catholic Church, but our Puritan forefathere, in their determination to he separatesl as much as possible from that church at the time of the Reormattori, tabood sod prohibited their exercise and stigmatized it as witchcraft and of the devil, and thus the prottent-day Proteetant Church has, by being bound by the dicta of their forefathers, " banged, bolted mid barred" the door against the oily evidence of an external nature which can successfully combat the materialistic and agnostic spirit of the age. div.p: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD
OPENS A NEW LIBERAL CLUB AT COLBORNE.
Speech on Current Politics.

Mr. A. IL Crookeld opened a new Liberal Club at Colborne on Saturday and was accorded a most enthusiastic reception by a large gathering of the pro- greasive. of the locality. Liberalism has not been without headquarters m Colborne in the past, but club premises have had to be rooted from a company! and there was a strong feeling amongst the members dist they should have a building which they could call their own. The new blab is pleasantly intwited and admirably adapted for recreative purposes, while provision is made for a first-class bowling green. The complete echeme will coat about X 11,10) Councillor W. "1. Slather presided at the opening ceremony and amongst others pretient were Councillors J. Naylor and A. Yates, Mr. Halliday, Mr. H. it. Rigby and Mr. H. New, of Warrington. Most of the speech-making took place from a temporary platform outside the club. . , . '

Mr. Croshold, who was greeted with applause, con- gratulated the Liberals of Holborn° upon their eaterpriae in erecting such a haudsome club and said he was particularly glad that a bowling green was to be pro- vided. lie had never been one to belittle outdoor recreation—(hear, besot—although he often thought that in England a great many people were inclined to lose then' balance and to treat outdoor sports as an end in themselves, instead of a means to an end. (Hear, hear.) lie hod bees very keen on •utdoor sports him- self Hlaughter)—aud he was not at all ashamed of the fact. Regarded in its right proportions such recreation was. excellent thing for the people of England. After all, happiness in a sensible way was as end in itself nod games contributed very much to happiness and good fellowship and helped to draw people together. (Rear, bear.) But that club would not only be a centre or social intercourse but would doubtless play au importaut part in maintaining Liberal tradi- tions and datseminating Liberal principles. Is these great and stirring times, they would lbud it educative and encouraging to discuss high affairs of litate within the walls of that building which public-spirited and courageous Liberals had provided. lie was not exaggerating in stating that the lest decade would rank Be probably the morn memorable years in all history. Wheal they considered research, invention, scienoe and art —tho progress in all 0080 great factors in our national late of recent yours bad been simply astonish- ing. Had our forelatners been told that humanity would make each advances in so short n period they would have laughed the idea to acorn. What was true of progress in other dopartmenta of lite was particularly true ol • ' '

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P. THE SHORTER WORKING DAY.

Reference was made at some length in column a few weeks back to the introduction into the House of Commons of a Bill for the gradual reduction of the hours of labour in cotton factories to 48 per week. I have known no more remarkable conversion in a record time than the change which has come over the leaders, or some of them, of the Lancashire textile operatives than their present enthusiasm for a4B hours week. It is not four years since the men who are now pressing forward this movement were opposing the reform with all the old argu- ments which had done duty in every campaign against shorter hours since the beginning of the last century. TWO IMPORTANT EVENTS.

Two things happened last week which should greatly stimulate the movement for a legal 48 hours week, or more properly speak- ing, a legal Eight Hours day. The one event is the passing into law of an Act for the reduction of the hours in the cotton factories of Massachusetts to 54 per week. This is one and a half hours a week less than the legal number in Great Britain, and by this enactment this country loses the honourable place it has held since the beginning of the factory system as being the country working the shortest number of hours. The reduc- tion of hours in Massachusetts is the more remarkable when it is remembered that it is only eighteen months since the last reduction, which brought the working week down Dom 58 to 56 hours, that is to say,that in eighteen months there has been a legal reduction of the factory hours by four per week. With the excep- tion of the reduction of one hour per week, the hours in the British factories have remained unchanged for more than a genera- tion. The reduction in Massachusetts has been carried out with the approval of both employers and workpeople. In other respects the Labour laws of this American State are in advance of those in Great Britain. The employees of public authorities have a legal eight hours day, and no child is allowed to work under 14 years of age, and unless it can produce a certificate of educational efficiency it must not be employed under 16 years of age. We shall have to look up and be moving, or we shall soon be left far behind in the matter of industrial legislation. THE INTERNATIONAL MOVEMENT. The second event of last week which is likely to help the movement in this country for a shorter working day is the decision of the International Textile Congress at Amsterdam in favour of an international movement for an Eight Hours Day. At previous Congresses there had been opposi- tion to this proposal, but on this occasion the resolution was passed unanimously and with great enthusiasm. It would, of course, make it easier to gain this boon if there could be an approximation of hours in the various countries, but the bold step which the State of Massachusetis has taken shows that there is no need to wait until the laggards have come into line. The State of Massachusetts has to face the competition of the cotton mills in the Southern States, where the raw material is close at hand, where there is practically no restriction of child labour, and where the hours of labour for adults are very much longer; and the State of Massachusetts enjoys no protection by tariffs against the competition of these Southern States. It is very gratifying to see that the great truth is being recognised and acted upon that low wages and long hours are had economically, and that it pays both employers and work- people to establish good and humane con- ditions of labour. A GREAT CAMPAIGN.

The Independent Labour Party is about to start a campaign in favour of a Minimum Wage of 30s. a week for all adult workers, and for a Universal Eight Hours day. It is very gratifying to me to see this question of a shorter working day coming into the front again. Fifteen and twenty years ago it was the most discussed question in the industrial world. It always figured in the resolution at every Labour and Socialist demonstration. ISo much importance was attached to it that ths engineers faced a seven months lock-out for the ideal. The defeat of the engineers in that great struggle seemed to dishearten the agitation, and for the last dozen years very little has been heard about the reform. A shorter working day is one of those industrial reforms which bring to the workers a benefit which cannot be filched away from them by any action of the employers; it is a reform which has not only great economic advan- tages, but physical and social advantages also.

div.head: MINERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE MINERS' STRIKE.

One hesitates to express an opinion on the decision of the Minors Federation Conference which last week decided to withdraw national support from the men who are out on strike in South Wales. In the opinion of the delegates to this conference the South Wales men should have accepted the terms of settlement which were arranged a few weeks ago, and which the officials of the South Wales Miners' had advised the men to accept. The situation in South Wales is critical in the extreme, and one cannot dis- cern a ray of hope in the darkness. The leaders are all at loggerheads, and the men are taking things into their own hands. The only people who are benefiting by this state of affairs are the mine owners, who must be exulting to themselves over the disunity which exists in the men's ranks. The with- drawal of national support from the Cambrian men takes away the last hope of success for them. The funds of the South /Vales Union are practically exhausted, and 12,000 men cannot be maintained without a very heavy coat.

div.head: 'BADLY MANAGED.
div.p: 'BADLY MANAGED.

....... The whole business seems to have been badly managed from the very beginning, and there seems no hope except to settle this trouble as best they can and then begin again to organise under leaders they can trust. This dispute has exposed the impotence of the Board of Trade to deal with such matters. In the early stages of the trouble Mr. Askwith made great efforts to bring the matter to a settlement, but with- out success. At the present time all parties are welcoming the signs of the coming sub- stitution of arbitration for war in the matter of international disputes, but here is an industrial war in our own borders, over which this nation has full authority, and which has been going on for nine months and which has involved as much hardship and suffering, apart from loss of life, as an ordinary war entails, and yet the nation and Parliament seem to be happily indifferent to it all.

div.head: FUTILE STRIKE.
div.p: THE FUTILE STRIKE.

_ Now that national support has been with- drawn from the Cambrian men, and in view of the internecine strife which is going on, and the probability that the (despair and anger of the men may find expression in undesirable ways, it seems a case in which

the Board of Trade ought to interfere. If its powers are not strong enough to bring this dispute to an end, then more power ought to be given to it. The dispute is bringing ruin to the Rhondda district, and it will be a long time before the effects of this disastrous stoppage have been wiped away. The state of affairs there is another instance of the futility of the strike except in rare circum- stances. The miners had a good case, but they had to faces very powerful cornbine of owners, and the struggle has been a test of the survival of the fittest; and the fittest to survive in such a struggle is the party which has unlimited resources. THE FIGHTING SEAMEN.

The Seamen's strike began badly. Some of the runners were so impatient that they started before the pistol went. But on the whole it has up to the present gone better and been more successful than could reason- ably have been expected. It has secured better conditions for the men on several of the great lines, but it has not yet made any impression on the owners of the tramp , vessels where the labour conditions are most in need of betterment. The seamen are a most difficult class to organise, and it is much easier to get a strike amongst them than it is to get them to remain permanently in an organisation. This strike is really for the purpose of getting the men better organised, and if it succeeds in that object it will have done even better service than if it succeeds in gaining some little present improvement in the rates of pay. Up to the time of writing, the strike really does appear to have done better than, I believe, some of the leaders antioipated. But the Shipping Federation is a very well organised body, and, as the men have reason to know, a body without any bowels of compassion, and if the men win in this fight it will be the first time they have beaten the Shipping Federation. There is no more deserving body of workers than the %ailors, and they deserve aneeena.

div.p: ST. HELENS.
OPERATIVE BAKERS' HOURS.
Mr. Pleb,' Swift, M.P., pr. sided on Saturday night over a largely attended puolic meeting at St. Helens Town Hell in support of the bakers Forty-eight Hour. Bill.

The Chairman said two conditions world appear to him to justify the State in interfering to limit the hours of labour—either that the work in which people were engage] was 'such as crippled the worker either tioyslcally r mentally it the hours were unduly long, or in cases in which the work if carried on for too long might affect and injure other persona. In rasel of child labour in factories or con- tinuous labour in tnides which dealt with poisons or with poisonous matter. the State ought to interfere. Outside these principles he was exceedingly loth to intstfore with the right, of it man to work as long as he liked to do. If it were shown that the Forty-eight Hours Bill was the best way of dealing with the vievances of the trade it must be supported. One or tw-i speakers dealt with the conditions of labour in bakehouses and the danger to the community from disease, and particularly Loos comutoption, which was so rife among the bakers. Mr. J. Hart (president of the St. Helens Trades and labour Council) moved a resolution calling upon the liovernment to give facilities for the iecond reading of thr.i.For.ty-?ight Hours liakebouae Bill.

Mr. J. Francis, eacmtary of the Trades Council, seconded, and said that many of the local bakehouses accrue diagram, to tbe tone. Mr. J. A. Seddon, es-M.P. for Newton, pointed out that during the last forty or lifty psore the production of each mutt in the trade had, by the application of machinery and science, been more than doubled, but the wages of the men had not been doubled ; in fact, in some cases they had gone down. that being so, it tram high time that the bakers. both by organisation and Parliamentary action, did something to improve their prlUtion. . .

The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. Rigby Swift, in reply to a vote of thanks, expressed its ernesement that the bitter+ had not corn- blued better or dune anything of a rotenone nature during the lest teenty years to obtain some redress f, r the grievances they hod heard so much about that afternoon. He tree glad that he had had the opportunity of hesring the speeches and learning as much, and he would give the hill his most esrneet, consideration, end hoped to do the best and the right thing when the matter cents before Parliament.

div.p: A SUBSIDENCE IN EGYPT-STREET.

A peculiar accident occurred in Egypt-street on Monday afternoon. A steam roller, weighing 15 tons, belonging to the Corporation,had been levelling the road when the earth suddenly gave way and one of the huge rollers sank several feet. Several hours elapsed before it i.ould be got out.

THE COIioNATION

One if "Uncle Caleb's" correspondents copied for the " Children's Corner" some amusing lines fore- casting how ere this we should all be "Coronation mail." Well, I most needs have my little say in relation to the all-absorbing topic, bat I will take care to avoid vain repetiCon. I have a good friend who has been singularly. fortunate in point of exceptional facilities for siewmg, not only Thur:day's historic scene in Westminster Abbey, but likewise the crown- ing of the late King. A Lancashire cotton manufac- turer and an old member of the choir of lOs own Parish Church, he has Icng enjoyed the personal friendship of Sir Frederick Bridge and other iv tluential inusiciaes, ,Xc., in London, and un both the great occasions now in question had the good fortune to be invited to join the A ',hey choir, to witness the cereincny, and to be renewed with souveniis of the event. THE AMPULLA.

Of the regalia usid in anointing the King, this is the most ancient part. for although the wings of the 'golden eagle represented the pedestal upon which it stands date only from the Stuart period,the body of the bitil a unmistakably traceable to the I Ithcentury.The oil is poured in at the beak, the bead being imacrewed for the purpoee. 'I hi' legend in relation to it is that ono night when in banishment at Lyons, Sir Thomas a Beckett was vayiug in church, when there al peered to him an angel, with a golden eagle and small vial, which lie gave to him, at the ramie time asid.iring him that all kings who should he anointed with the oil in the vial would enjoy great happiness. St. Thomas was commanded to carry them to Pc tiers and to give them into the hands of a monk, who would conceal them beneath a certain stone in the Church of St. Gregory. That was done, arid the ampulla and the oil, with an account of his vision writtec. by St. Thomas, were preserved until the time • ' of Edward III.; when their hiding-place was revealed to a holy man in a dream. The finder took the treasures to the Black l'rince. and they were sent at first to the Tower of London for nab keeping. The sacred oil was not, however, used tint I the Coronation of Ilenry IV. in Gitfti. As to the magnificent sing placed on the King's right hand fourth finger to symboliee His Majesty'. marriage to his people, the ' story as it was told in the " Golden Legend " over lINI years ago is that it belonged to Edo and the Con- fessor, who one day gave it to" a certain fay re olde mail' who had asked lam for alms. Years alter, two English pilgrims in the Holy Land, who Lad hst their way, fell in with " a fayre auneyent man wyth whyte beer for age." Learning that they were from England, tl.e old man " comforted theym goodly, and brought into a feyre cytee." Ile gave them refresh- ment and a lodging, and in tho morning put them in the right way again. When the moment came for parting, the old man charg,el them to return to theyr Kynge Sayot Edward," to greet him well and to return to him the riag which the King had given him with bin own bards. The pilgrims brought the' ring safely to England. and it ever since been I. carefully preserved at Westniinater. THE KING'S ELDER BROTHER.

In reviewing Thursday's proceedings one naturally thinks ii the circumstances under which His Majesty came into the direct into of tuccession to the throne' through the death if ills brother, the Duke of Clarence ' some Itt years ago. Just before his fatal illness, I. reported a military function in which that lamented , Prince played a prominent part. His Royal Iliglinees came to the town in with 1 then was, and formally presented colours to a heal regiment. Curiously eniwalt the incidents in connection with the affair, winch stand cotta my memory were quite truing and ineignificant, having mainly to do with the self-: importance of sundry and diver, fussy individuals mote or less prominently ansotiated with the day's doings. Naturally, these were greatly scandalised by the behavicur of an enterprising pliotogiaplier, who just when all was in rear:mess for the final march pact of the troop., and the Ptince had taken up his pa,ition at the saluting point, with cool effrontery advanced a few yards from the crowd and planted his camera-tripod immediately in front of the too self- . conscious and plainly uncomfortable Ileir-Apparent. The officer in command roared is vain at the impudent photo-man, and it was t eceassry to ride up to the fellow and drive him off the field by main force. This Imy the way. Next news the Duke of Clarence anal dead, and in a manner specially Emphasised during the last few days, the whole course at English history was permanently changed. A PESSIMISTIC NOTE.

A journalist to wheat she I, sp pened to be under considerable obligation asked or to introduce him to Sir Henry Irving. Unfortunately. she had forgotten the pressman's name. so she pre- tended that they bail had a dispute as to the precise spelling and asked the newspaper representative to settle the point by writing it down for her. Refresh- ing her memory by a glance at the paper, Miss Terry clapped her hands and exclaimed, " Ah, I've won the bet," and proceeded with the introduction. That sort of device does not always act so well. I remember another irstance of a similar character, andon the absent.mioded one mildly enquiring " Let me Fee, bow spell your name ! Yes, yes; the Smiths we have always with tn. I well remember how, a chile ago, when the list of jurymen was called over at Burnley Sea Cone, out of the twelve selected no fewer than ten boasted of the name of Smith. or did this exhaust the visible supply of Smiths. When it was intimated by the Clerk of the Peace that those jurymen whose names c ere not called cut were not required, and forthwith proceeded to call for, say, 1% il him Smith, be was promptly requested in at least two places further to identify the particular Smith required, sod this the learned Clerk did by giving cut the address. The prisoners tried by that jury enjoyed—or others se—a probably unique expetience in being tried by ten Smiths. LOVERS OF DARKNESS.

. ..... . I suppose there is a time in the lives of moat people when a lot g tunnel is regarded by members of both sexes as a pleasant enough break in the naonmoi y of a railway excursicn. I recall such a ti ip when the prospective father-in-law f two 3 oung men in the party was careful at each tunnel to illuminate the compartment be means of a wax candle—lest, as he explained, his daughters shoed suffer from fright ! If it boil been permissible to cross-examine the said gentlemen, one would have liked to ask him if he 10..1 himself been young. if, when in his twenties, he had ever taken his sweet- heart to the seaside or elsewhere, if on such i tensions lie had not preferred a carriage without light, and what he would have thought of anybody who whenever a tunnel was entered had played the 'part of marplot and spoil sport by striking matches, to say nothing if deliberately providing a candle ! It w.,s the Photographic Society's summer astir g by canal boat that set my thoughts in this direction. I assume that is was a mixed party. Jted imagine then that three-quarter mile turniel between Preston Brook and Dutton. while yet no " camera shutters were heard clicking." But p.ssibly papa was there with his hateful matchbox and ridiculous bit of candle. TARIFF REFOlthf.

An acquaintance of mine who has a gift for open- air oratory, and, being an ardent and earnest tempera, ce ads coats, has long been in the habit of taking a spin on his bicycle and spending an evening here and there in exhorting to total abstinence such as step to listen to his rosy addresses, tel:s me that he has bean piomised £2,11, a year and expenses to devote his lane and talents to an outdoor campaign in favour of Tariff Reform. However being a convinced Free Trader, and having a conscience that will not suffer him to argue against c,nviction, lie has declined the flattering offer.

AMON(i THE SPOOKS. 'those nho went to the Druid's Hall when Mr. Tom Tyrrell was there the other day seem to have Leen mote fortunate than has been my lot when I have' companied with Spiritualists. I began my coped- moor, stout most unfortunately as it pm et!, with the notorious Dr. Monk, who was rent to gaol as an impostor ; and when I asked those who had invited me what they then thought of the system they had espoused, they simply pointed out that there were black sheep iii every flock, and continued to invite me. I accepted repeatedly. but never met a medium who was nearly so successful no the late visitor from Illsekborn scent, to have been here. At one seance which I attended, Alderman was present. and when a lady medium professed desmibe a spirit hovering over the aldermanic shoulder, the worthy magistrate no far forgot himself as to audibly exclaim, " Nowt etle sort !" .lOWNELEY BAIL.

Last Saturday, I went to Ti work!, Park near / Dummy- a fine old spot, with a history ; and, inci- dentally, 1 was kept a prioner on the little wayside station for fully all hour and a half, owing to a heavy thunderstorm, accompanied by a deluge of rain and hailstones. The Hall is now in the hands of the municipality, and there is a good picture gallery, though there appears to me to be danger of overdoing portraits in oil. Past mayors and other mrotbers of the Town Council, two or three in

I%,urt dress, look down upon one from life-size and they certainly are becoming so numercus as to create a sense of utter disproportion. Such things are all Tory well in newspapers now and again ; in the " Examiner '' I find them brought to such perfection as to be altogether admirable ; but. as I once heard the late Oscar Wilde say. one should not hang too many portraits for wall adornment, unleas the subjects he highly decorative—and that they seldom are.

div.head: CORONATIC N DAY. 1..11 Celebrated in Warrington and District THE KING'S MESSAGE TO OLD AGE PENSIONERS.
div.p: CORONATIC N DAY. 1..11 Celebrated in Warrington and District THE KING'S MESSAGE TO OLD AGE PENSIONERS.

Warrington jdned in the mighty (horns of loyally and enthusiasm which went up from every part of the British Dominions in llanteday when the atterition eta!! the Erglioh speaking world was,in imagination, concentrated upon the historic ceremony of the I Coronation of their Map sties King George and Queen I Mary, then heing enacted within the ancient and hallowed walls of Westminster Abbey. The pro- gramme of celebrations in or ancient borough, low- tier, was not quite so elaberate or impressive as the majority of the inhabitants would have wished. As far as the general public were concerned, there was only a somewhat sombre end uninspiring procession to watch in the morning, and for the remainder if the day they were left entirely to their own devices. Naturally considerable disappointment was espreesed that the lentil hies were not on a more lavish scale. The day woe not one calculated to live in the memory as historic and—most unhrturrate of all— the children had no celebrations of their own on Coronation Day, but had to be satisfied to play the part of spectators ifs demonstration which could not have appealed to them very much. It wan,however. a happy thought whiih prompted the provision of a : treat fox the old age pensioners of the borough, and I this feature of the celebrations can he unreserved'y commended. The aged guests were coked after with the utmost solicitude and spent a thoroughly enjoy- ' able time. Haying accepted an invitation to attend the ceremony in Westminster Abbey, the Meyer (Councillor Dr, Joeeph) was unable to take part in the local fes'ivities en Thursday. Ile was, however, worthily represented by the Deputy Mayor (Alderman Forslinw) who did

see repeated and possibly enlarged. The meeting that afternoon was eomigh to put heart into everybody. net they could produce no large a number in the little village of Stockton Heath wan eminently creditable. Ty were there to say ho. much they rejoined in their King, in his oplendid spirit of devotion end diligence to the high deter which had descended to hi. care. Ile (Mr Yongeitrusted that as they vent on they might find their differences tinting and be able to come togetber—Chtirch people and Nooconformista—with coidielity and mutual confidence in each other. (Appiau.). The service concluded eith the oinging of the National Anthem. .

A procession wee then formed, under the direction of Mr I, Rose, chief marshal. 'they marched in the follow. inn order —The Church lads' Brigade ; Mr Westbrook, Rev J Collins, M.A., Re• J Yonne, Rev If A Leaner, M.A., committee ,90 in number), bend, girls, infants in vehicles), hoys, pirlsbioners generally, ho? scouts, Order of R.A.0.8., 1.0.0. Children to the number of 1,350 were then served with a substantial tea in the Chrirchroorn, Church schools rind Council schools respectively, and each Add was presented e ith a handsome Coronation mug, which will not van perpetual reminder of the Corona- tion of King Deorge V.
